newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude called lower after shorts squeezed out.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude called lower after shorts squeezed out.

text.p: NYMEX crude was called lower Wednesday consolidating sharp gains made Tuesday on short covering ahead of the May refined product contract expiration today amid tight heating oil supply in the New York Harbor.
Bearish oil inventory data was also seen weighing on the market. Crude was called five to ten cents a barrel lower Refined products were called steady to off 0.25 cent a gallon.

"We are looking to correct today. The stock data could be bearish because while RFG (reformulated gasoline) stocks were down, the strong builds in crude could take center stage," said a New York crude trader.
On Tuesday, May heating oil ended up 2.38 cents a gallon at 58.91 cents. June crude finished up 53 cents at $20.44 a barrel while May gasoline ended up 1.02 cents a gallon at 63.36 cents.

Cash supplies of heating oil in the New York Harbor have been tight after unseasonably cold weather in the northeastern United States drained refinery stocks. The region is the largest heating oil market in the world.
With the May heating oil contract expiring amid short supply, traders bought themselves out of their short positions which would have obligated them to deliver heating oil.

After the market's close, the American Petroleum Institute (API) released oil inventory data for the week ended April 25. Gasoline stocks fell 408,000 barrels and distillate stocks drew 1.4 million barrels, both declining as traders expected.

The U.S. Department of Energy's Energy Information Administration (EIA) in its own data for the same period said on Wednesday that gasoline stocks grew 100,000. But, it said reformulated gasoline gasoline stocks, the gasoline deliverable against the NYMEX contract, declined 1.7 million barrels.
The DOE also said crude stocks grew about million barrels more than the 1.87 million barrel build reported by the API.
"The DOE's were a bit more bearish for the crude, so that should pressure the market, otherwise gasoline would be leading us higher," said a New York dealer.
